title: Code interception protection
lesson: An intercepted authorization code cannot be redeemed without its private PKCE verifier.
corrections: At 13.1s replace the overly specific invalid_grant label for an absent verifier with NO TOKEN.
Fade the full frame at both endpoints; use bounded FFmpeg threads and attenuated AAC for reproducible delivery.
At 9.0–9.8s move the intercepted-code chip below the actor labels to avoid transient overlap.
transcript: 0–7s: The mobile app retains a verifier and sends its S256 challenge. The server binds a newly issued authorization code to that challenge.
8–15s: An interceptor gets the code but not the verifier. Its token request is rejected.
16–22s: The legitimate app supplies the verifier. The server checks the challenge, consumes the code and returns the access token.
limitations: The mobile-app interception example complements the chapter’s agent-host concurrency example.
Browser consent, redirects, TLS and other OAuth checks are omitted. Token issuance assumes those checks pass.
The final legitimate redemption illustrates possession of the correct verifier; do not assume every server preserves a code after a rejected exchange. Start a fresh attempt when needed.
NO TOKEN describes rejection without prescribing a provider-specific missing-verifier error.
